findings.counterexample: `Write-Output '<#' ; sed -i 's/a\t/b/' f` (PowerShell) — expected deny(sed-i-escape); actual at b0f8c901 allow; at 01351edd deny. PowerShell ground truth (powershell.exe): `Write-Output '<#'` / `Write-Output 'MIDDLE-RAN'` / `Write-Output '#>'` prints all three lines — the middle command runs.

findings.counterexample: `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 gh pr view 1; git show $(echo origin/main:a.md)` (win32) — per the sentence no warn; actual warn(msys-rev-path-subshell).

findings.claim: `sedHasScriptFile` read `-f` only as a token's first character, so a clustered short option (`-nf`, `-Enf`) was not a script file — a pre-existing false positive the widened doc line did not disclose.
findings.counterexample: `sed -i -nf 'C:\t.sed' file` — GNU 4.9 reads `-n` + `-f C:\t.sed`, no expression operand; expected allow; actual deny with the script path as the fragment (both daae514b and b0f8c901).

findings.claim: An operand after `--` that begins with `-f` is read as a script file though `--` ended option parsing — an undisclosed over-allow (the leg's 'GNU rejects it' rationale was itself wrong: BRd-F3).
findings.counterexample: `sed -i -- -fx` — the scanner returns no expressions → allow.

findings.claim: The blanker's new comment-start set `/[\s;|(){}&,]/` was strictly wider than the scanners' rule it claimed to reuse (WORD_BOUNDARY plus paren provenance), so on `{`, `}`, `,`, `\f`, `\v` and a substitution-closing `)` the blanker declared a comment where the scanners read code, left a same-line `<# … #>` block unblanked, and handed it to the scanners as code — a charter positive PowerShell executes was dropped and a command PowerShell never runs was denied.
findings.counterexample: MISS: `Write-Output $(1)#c <# it's #>` + newline + `sed -i 's/\r$//' f` (PowerShell) — powershell.exe prints `1` then runs the sed; daae514b denied, 65332be1 allowed. FALSE DENY: `Write-Output $(1)#c <# ; sed -i 's/\r$//' f #>` — powershell.exe prints `1` and the tail, the sed never runs; 65332be1 denied.

findings.claim: The header's sentence 'skips its `#` line comments by the same token-start rule the scanners apply, so the two never disagree about which text is code' was false in both halves: the sets differed in source, and PowerShell itself begins a comment after a closing quote or an `=` where neither model did.
findings.counterexample: The BRd-F1 payloads; `Write-Output 'a'#b; Write-Output TAIL` prints only `a` under powershell.exe; `$x=#c` swallows the next line.

findings.claim: The `--` disclosure's safety rationale ('a command GNU sed itself rejects') was false: GNU sed 4.9 edits `./-file` in place, and the widened regex extended the over-allow to `-nfile`, `-zfile`, `-Enfile` after `--`, each of which the previous head denied.
findings.counterexample: `printf 'aXb\n' > ./-file; sed -i -- 's/X/Q/' -file` → rc=0, `aQb`. `sed -i -- 's/a\t/b/' -nfile` — daae514b deny, 65332be1 allow.

findings.claim: Two sub-assertions inside the two termination-check `it` blocks do not discriminate against daae514b (the `a#b` guard; the `-if` guard); whole-block discrimination intact at 4 of 42.
findings.counterexample: Measured pre=head for both.

findings.claim: The unification's `=` comment-start rule was unconditional; PowerShell begins a comment after `=` only for the assignment operator, so an argument token carrying `=#` was discarded as a comment and the statement PowerShell executes was hidden.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output a=#b ; sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` (PowerShell) — PSParser: CommandArgument(a=#b) then Command(sed); powershell.exe prints `a=#b` then runs the sed; expected deny, 20e0ca20 allowed, 65332be1 denied. Same for `http://h/p?a=#t`, `--define=#fff`.

findings.claim: The closing-quote comment-start rule fired after ANY closing quote; PowerShell starts a comment there only when the quote BEGAN the token.
findings.counterexample: `x='a'#c ; sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` — PSParser: Command(x=a#c) StatementSeparator(;) Command(sed); the sed runs; expected deny, 20e0ca20 allowed. Control `Write-Output 'a'#c ; sed …` — PSParser: String(a) Comment(…); allow is correct.

findings.claim: `substitutionEnd` counted parens over quotes only and knew nothing about `<# … #>`, so a `)` inside a block comment closed a `$( … )` early and the orphaned `#>` started a line comment that swallowed the rest — a second model of `<#` inside the unified walk.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output $(1 <# ) #>) ; sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` — PSParser: GroupStart Number Comment(<# ) #>) GroupEnd then Command(sed); powershell.exe prints `1` and runs the sed; expected deny, 20e0ca20 allowed.

findings.claim: The header's rationale 'PowerShell ends a token at a string or an `=`; bash does not' (restated in the ScanOptions docblock, the changeset, the spec and the test comment) was false against PSParser: only a token-starting string and the assignment operator end a token.
findings.counterexample: PSParser on `Write-Output a=#b` → CommandArgument(a=#b); on `x='a'#c` → Command(x=a#c).

findings.claim: The unification's new test pinned only the two shapes where PowerShell agrees with the over-broad rules and none from the sibling class where it disagrees, so the suite was green while the contract clause was false.
findings.counterexample: Adding `run("x='a'#c ; sed …")` or `run('Write-Output a=#b ; sed …')` to the block failed at 20e0ca20 while its five assertions passed.

findings.claim: On `<<#` the tokenizer's `<#` branch matches at the second `<` while findHeredocs takes the `<<` heredoc branch and reads `#` as a bare delimiter — an intra-fold disagreement on a command PowerShell refuses to parse (`The terminator '#>' is missing`).
findings.counterexample: `cat <<#\nx\d\nEOF` (PowerShell): HEAD deny/heredoc-escape, 65332be1 allow; nothing runnable is denied.

findings.claim: The precise `=` rule still fired in argument position, where PowerShell has no assignment operator and `=` is an ordinary character of a CommandArgument, so a `#` PowerShell does not read as a comment hid a real `sed -i`.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output $x=#c ; sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` — PSParser: CommandArgument($x=#c) StatementSeparator(;) Command(sed); powershell.exe runs the sed; expected deny, 97c33663 allowed. Same for `Write-Output $(1)=#c`, `Write-Output =#c`, `$x==#c`.

findings.claim: The token-start proxy was bash's word, not PowerShell's token: after `$x=` the following string IS its own token and adjacent strings are separate tokens, so eight everyday PowerShell assignments with a trailing comment moved from allow to deny.
findings.counterexample: `$x='a'#c ; sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` — PSParser: Variable(x) Operator(=) String(a) Comment(…); the sed never runs; expected allow, 97c33663 denied. Same for `$x="a"#c`, `$x+='a'#c`, `$env:X='a'#c`, `$x[0]='a'#c`, `Write-Output "a"'b'#c`.

findings.claim: The ScanOptions docblock's '`''` and `""` read as two adjacent strings under both grammars' was false for PowerShell, where they are one token with an embedded quote, and the fold had made that sentence load-bearing.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output 'a''b'#c ; sed …` — PSParser: String(a'b) Comment(…); expected allow, 97c33663 denied.

findings.claim: The two scanners carried different predicates for the same rules and disagreed on 7 of 18 probed shapes; findHeredocs read a stale word head from the previous word.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output "a"=#c ; cat > f <<'EOF'\nre /\d/\nEOF` → allow (findHeredocs) while the sed sibling denied; `$x \a=#c ; cat …` vs `Write-Output \a=#c ; cat …` differed only in the previous word's head.

findings.claim: The spec's 'the same rules apply inside a `$( … )`' overstated substitutionEnd, which implements only the block-comment skip and the backtick escape.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output $(Write-Output 'a'#) ; sed …` — a command PowerShell refuses to parse; the scanner closes the substitution and denies; the clause is what was wrong.

findings.claim: PowerShell also ends a token at the `)` closing a `$( … )`, so `$(1)#c` is a comment there while the scanners apply bash's rule; unchanged since the unification and fail-closed.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output $(1)#c ; sed …` — PSParser: GroupEnd Comment; the sed never runs; the scanner denies.

findings.claim: The withdrawal's disclosure bounded the miss direction to one carrier ('an odd quote') while a `<#`, a trailing backslash and an unterminated `$(` in the same-line comment produce the same execution-confirmed miss; six of those moved from deny to allow at the withdrawal and the pinned test covered only the odd-quote carrier.
findings.counterexample: `Write-Output 'a'#note <#` + newline + `sed -i 's/\d/x/' f` — PSParser: String(a) Comment(#note <#) NewLine Command(sed); powershell.exe prints `a` then runs the sed; 97c33663 denied, 9bb34073 allowed. A 4-arm × 8-carrier sweep: 15 misses over 5 carriers.

findings.claim: A doubled conjunction ('and and') survived the rewrite in the changeset and the spec.
findings.counterexample: Verbatim at both sites.

findings.claim: The header's illustrative pair was mis-matched: `a=#b` reads the same in both statement positions; the pair that differs only by statement position is `$x=#c` (an assignment plus a comment) versus `Write-Output $x=#c` (one argument).
findings.counterexample: PSParser: `a=#b ; sed …` → Command(a=#b); `Write-Output a=#c ; sed …` → CommandArgument(a=#c) — the same reading.

findings.claim: 'five successive attempts to model them [token boundaries]' held only under the broad reading 'which text is code': the pre-pass and its string tracking carried no token-boundary rule; the strict count is three.
findings.counterexample: git log: b0f8c901 and daae514b (the pre-pass and its string tracking), then 65332be1, 20e0ca20, 97c33663 (the three token-boundary models).

withdrawn: The two PowerShell comment-start rules (a string that began its token; the assignment operator) were withdrawn at 9bb34073 rather than refined a sixth time: PowerShell's token boundaries are not derivable from a character walk (`a=#b` and `$x=#c` differ only by statement position; `'a'#b` and `x='a'#c` only by where the token began), and each of five successive models opened a sibling shape. A `#` is read by bash's word-boundary rule for both tools; the residual — a `#` after a token-ending string, an assignment operator or a `)` — is word text to the scanners, the over-scan direction, except a same-line comment carrying an odd quote before a later positive, the one miss, disclosed in the header and pinned as a test.

designNote: Three BLOCKING faults in three successive folds of one pre-pass, each a disagreement between the pre-pass and the scanners about which text is code, were taken as the evidence that a second model cannot be kept in agreement with the first. The fold at 20e0ca20 deletes the pre-pass: ScanOptions.powershell threads from payload.tool through findHeredocs and tokenizeShell, which read PowerShell's grammar where it differs (block comments, the backtick escape, a comment after a closing quote or an `=`) in the same walk that tracks quotes and comments. The Bash-tool verdicts are unchanged by construction: the flag is off.
disclosedNotFolded: PowerShell here-strings (`@" … "@`, `@' … '@`) are not parsed (header comment)
an export inside a subshell `( … )` or a pipeline element is taken as reaching later segments though the shell would not apply it — the over-allow direction (header comment, changeset, spec)
a wrapper that takes operands of its own before the program (sudo -u me, timeout N, npx) hides the program from the position anchor (header comment)
a heredoc inside a `bash -c "…"` / `sh -c '…'` operand is not recursed into (header comment)
a partly quoted heredoc delimiter (`E'O'F`) is read to its first quote — over-scan (HEREDOC_AT comment)
verdict: TERMINATED at 45cbce223f75d11ccbaa682d6e4164cbf40b60c8 (claude-opus-5[1m], six legs on the bot round): re-armed over b0f8c901 — BLOCKING 1 · MATERIAL 3 · MINOR 5, folded in daae514b; termination check over daae514b — BLOCKING 1 · MATERIAL 2 · MINOR 3, folded in 65332be1; over 65332be1 — BLOCKING 1 · MATERIAL 2 · MINOR 1, the pre-pass deleted in 20e0ca20; over 20e0ca20 — BLOCKING 3 · MATERIAL 2 · MINOR 1, folded in 97c33663; over 97c33663 — BLOCKING 1 · MATERIAL 3 · MINOR 2, the two comment-start rules withdrawn in 9bb34073; over 9bb34073 — MATERIAL 1 · MINOR 3, prose only, folded at the head this deposit names. 35 findings: 28 folded in code or prose, 1 corrected out of band, 6 named. The Bash-tool verdicts were unchanged through every pass (differential sweeps of 612, 1,064 and 1,640 payloads, zero transitions beyond the one intended sed fix). What the bot round leaves the gate with: Gemini's two quote-aware scans, Greptile's block-comment bypass closed and its eject ownership fixed, CodeRabbit's eleven folds; and one design decision on the record — PowerShell's token boundaries are disclosed, not modelled. The PR is presented for the merge word on this record.
